newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Cockerill seen plunging into loss.
newsitem.headline: Cockerill seen plunging into loss.

text.p: Belgian steel maker Cockerill Sambre is expected to announce on Wednesday it plunged into loss in 1996, battered by falling steel prices in the second half.

However, analysts say Cockerill shares have discounted poor results, and consider the stock a "hold" or "speculative buy" with prices already rising for hot galvanised steel and expected to pick up soon for Cockerill's other flat products.
In 1995, when German unit Eko Stahl was consolidated for the first time, Cockerill made a group net profit of 3.2 billion francs after 800 million profit in 1994.
But it slipped into the red in the first half of 1996 with a group loss of 180 million francs after a previous 3.1 billion profit.
Analysts forecast a current group loss for full year 1996 of about two billion francs, after hearing gloomy comments from the company's management in January this year.
"They told us that the second half would be more disappointing than the first half," said Olivier Heuschling, sector analyst at Banque Bruxelles Lambert (BBL).
Prices had fallen in the second half, even though volumes remained good, partly due to client destocking and partly due to the general economic environment.

Also weighing on results would be Cockerill's German car components unit Ymos AG, which he expected to have a loss of about one billion francs, and mechanical unit CMI, where losses were forecast at about 500 million francs.

"I expect CMI booked a loss as forecast, but things are improving -- they've got a lot of orders and the problems are mostly over," Generale Bank analyst Loic de Caters noted. "Ymos is no longer a strategic activity for Cockerill," he added.
On the positive side a "substantial" capital gain is expected on the sale of Ymos's locking systems division to French group Valeo last September.

But analysts say large provisions might be made in 1996 for Cockerill's "Horizon 2000" restructuring plan in Belgium which aims to cut production costs and improve flexibility. About 2,000 jobs will be lost over three years.

Philippe Koeckx at Reyers, Timmermans forecast a current group loss of between 700 million and one billion francs, at the lower end of the range of forecasts. "It's clear there will (also) be restructuring provisions," he added.
Thierry Hazevoets, a market analyst at BBL/Vermeulen Raemdonck said Cockerill shares were a "speculative buy".
They should benefit from the fact that about 80 percent of the company's galvanised steel prices were spot prices, so the company was not greatly locked into unfavourable contract prices.
Also the dollar's surge of over 10 percent since the end of 1996 meant it was less attractive for the United States to export to Europe, but favourable for Europeans to export.
"Prices should go up -- volumes are very good. Then we could re-rate the stock," he said, adding that 150 francs was his short term target.
Cockerill shares, being privileged, also offer the prospect of three statutory 12 franc gross dividends to be paid by 1999.
"Not many people expect a dividend this year. We'd expect an 18-franc dividend each in June 1998 and 1999," Hazevoets said.
De Caters at Generale Bank said the effects of higher prices should begin to show in second half 1997 earnings, adding: "In the short term, Cockerill shares have recovery potential."

By midday on the Brussels bourse on Tuesday Cockerill shares were one franc higher at 126. The heavily cyclical shares touched a two-and-a-half-year low of 112 francs last December after peaking in September 1994 at 214 francs.
